But three of the Muslims who were executed in this incident and one of the survivors of that execution were under age at the time and, in fact, Armin Bazdar who survived the killing was only just 15. These people weren't subjects for prosecution. These were just Muslim children; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Well, 15 years or 150 years, if somebody was suspected of having committed crimes, they were brought in regardless of their age. I'm sorry that little Armin Bazdar was among them. And of course it turned out that he was innocent and he survived, and I am delighted at that. As for the rest, I really cannot say anything more because I was not in charge of the prison. There were other people responsible for that. I just dropped by on three occasions. I spent half an hour there, Vujic Mirko, my relative, was among the detainees. I just wanted to see how they were faring. I did not know that anyone was killed before they were transferred by truck. So you should not ask me to confirm something that I really don't know about. All I can speak of under oath is something that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Ujic, just to be clear you told the Bosnian court that you knew about this execution either the day it happened or the next day. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly true. The same day or the next day I heard that it had happened, and I was shocked. I asked myself: Why? Why? Why? And I'm still wondering: Why? For whose benefit was that? On whose order was that? That was done on someone's own initiative, and I don't know whether the command brigade is responsible or the individual who was convicted for that and is now serving a sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to go now to 65 ter 24462. While that's coming up, Mr. Ujic, the Rogatica Brigade was generally commended by the superior command for its activities during 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes, because it managed to preserve the territory, it managed to prevent the announced genocide and killings; and in that period very bad things were happening in Rogatica. So there was no exodus, there were no mass killings, and probably that was the reason why they were commended by the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see here a 26 December 1992 commendation from the SRK commander Stanislav Galic to the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade command and the Rogatica Brigade command, referring to the "great and immeasurable contribution of your fighters and units and "the Army of Republika Srpska's magnificent successes in 1992. Congratulating you on what has been achieved, let these successes be a stimulus for you to continue with the successes in 1993, until the realisation of the just goals of our struggle - freedom and a life worthy of man in Republika Srpska." This is a reflection of the superior command's approval of the Rogatica Brigade's activity in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: If I were to deny that, it would be irresponsible and ridiculous. If the corps command phrased it that way, then it must be like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6108, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. I have a few questions. Let me start with the latest one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 50 you said that you had learned about the event on that very same day or the following day. How did you learn about that? Did you receive any official report or in what way?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, as a brigade officer I had a hand-held radio set and an RUP-12 radio station in my vehicle. Through these communications devices, I heard a conversation between the local Kozici unit commander and that is how I learned about it. When I went to the scene, I saw that and I returned totally disappointed in war and in everything because that was completely contrary to all my visions and ideas. And we were trained and these instructions came from you as well, that we should treat soldiers according to international conventions. But it was impossible to persuade certain individuals to abide by these rules, and everybody should be responsible for their own acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who suggested that this was done by extremists and when did you learn the real name of the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: I did not know his name for a long time. Initially I was told that that was done by the White Eagles, Arkan's men, Seselj's men, et cetera. After some investigation a few days later, we did find out that Mr. Paunovic, aka Spiro, was the perpetrator who was the platoon commander and his task was to unblock this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you or anyone else, if you know, inform me or anyone else at Pale about this incident?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I did not. Whether somebody else reported this to you, I really don't know. If they did, I would like to know who it was. If not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 38 of today's transcript you were asked about the civilian population, about the secondary school centre. So can we briefly look at -- and you said that that was a reception centre for civilian population. So can we please look at P5485, that's a Prosecution exhibit and that's a regular combat report compiled by Mr. Kusic. Mr. Ujic, please look at the second sentence, where it says that a lot of Muslims are arriving in the town every day, mostly women and children, and they are being accommodated in the secondary school centre. Is this consistent with what you knew?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I knew, and I keep saying here in this courtroom that the secondary school was not a concentration camp. It was, I reiterate, a safe house for people to find shelter and avoid becoming casualties unnecessarily. So whoever wrote this should stand by it and that was the truth. The Muslims themselves wanted us to provide them safe haven where they would feel secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What do you say about this where he says that they are arriving? Does that mean that somebody was bringing them in or did they arrive of their own volition?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Most of them arrived of their own volition. I only noticed two armed soldiers who escorted them safely to the school. However, I did see columns without any military escort whatsoever heading for the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today you said that the leadership requested and the leadership made the same request to abide by international conventions. In that respect I need document 1D04177. I'm not sure if it's been translated, albeit it's being sent for translation a long time ago. Today when asked about the SRK command approving the actions of Rogatica Brigade, can you tell me did the SRK command approve this killing?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: I can categorically ascertain that they didn't, not the brigade command, not the corps command, nor the Supreme Command, nobody officially approved of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at this letter that was sent by the president of Rogatica municipality on the 25th of November, 1992, I'm talking about Mr. Tomislav Batinic, commander of Rogatica Brigade. And he says here, I'm going to read the first paragraph: "The Presidency of Republika Srpska sent a telex to the Municipal Assembly of Rogatica on the 9th of November, in 1999 [as interpreted], in which they reminded them of their responsibility for the events taking place in the territory of their municipality with respect to possible breaches of international humanitarian law, with regard to treatment of war prisoners. "It has been pointed out that civilians cannot be detained against their will, the civilians who hadn't committed any crimes, and that they had to be safely released and escorted to the territory that they wished to go. This does not pertain only to the women, children, and the elderly, but also to the sick enemy soldiers ..." et cetera. Do you remember this instruction?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: I remember it clearly, and as I said you yourself - as the president and the Commander-in-Chief - issued warnings that we should respect all the international conventions governing warfare and that we should treat prisoners of war in a proper manner. This letter is a confirmation of that because I kept saying here that we really wanted to avoid any casualty that was unnecessary. Of course, in any war people get killed. It's quite clear. However, if you manage to reduce the number of victims or casualties is a success in itself, and we did our best to reduce that number as much as possible. But as I said, there are victims in every war. I already said that the civilians were given forms to fill out to say where they wanted to go. Some of them wanted to go and reunite with their families in Tuzla, some wanted to go to Skopje and other places and towns. I also know that buses were secured to transport them to their destinations under the police escort. Another example, one of those people named Katica Musan, who was detained at Rasadnik from Bujata [phoen] village, the village was loyal, because of fear of revenge and with their consent we transferred them to the school. Later on, the same person, Katica Musan, begged us not to be sent to Sarajevo because he was going to be killed by his own people. Unfortunately, he had to be exchanged, to go to Sarajevo, and his own son killed him. This is what I heard three days after his departure. He was alive and well while he was with us. As soon as he went to Sarajevo, his own son killed him on his door-step.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What does it say here further on? Is there again a reference to the Geneva Conventions that the Red Cross should have access to everything, and it also says that the president of the Municipal Assembly has to provide information to the Presidency of the republic on the existence of prisons and collection centres in the area of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2913, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 7435 would be the 65 ter number that I'd like to have called up now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what then Captain Kusic responded to the president of the municipality. Let us take a look at the first paragraph. It says that this is a reply to the letter sent on the 25th of November, 1992. It says: "Since the first day of combat activities, the members of the Rogatica Brigade have treated the civilian population according to the Geneva Conventions. We have separated civilian population from extreme combatants we have fought against. With your approval, we have gathered civilians at the secondary school, the church centre, and the DP 'Ergela' in Rogatica building. In accordance with the circumstances involved, we were providing them with the same food our soldiers on the front line received three times a day." Is this correct, what the first paragraph says?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: All of this is correct, each and every letter written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the third paragraph, the last sentence, says: "With a view to protecting their lives from Muslim extremists because they expressed their loyalty to the Serb municipality of Rogatica." What can you tell us about that? What was the attitude taken towards Muslims who did not want to fight and who stayed in the villages? What was the attitude of the extremists, the Muslim extremists?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Well, the extremists Muslims who were warriors, if I can put it that way, who engaged in combat - I state this with full responsibility - they hated those loyal Muslims more than Serbs because they considered them to be their own national traitors. We had to protect these loyal Muslims more from their extremists than from our own troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they do anything in these villages, in these loyal villages or around these loyal villages, these Muslim extremists do something?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they tried through incursions, threats, intimidation, looting; however, when we moved the defence lines from those villages then they couldn't reach those households any longer. So later on these people managed to live in peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, no objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2914, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 25 you were asked about the Territorial Defence and local communes. Can you tell us in terms of the organisation and mobilisation of the Territorial Defence in all socio-political communities, local communes included, was there anything done then that was in contravention of the laws that were then in force?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility to the best of my knowledge that not in a single local commune, regardless of whether there was Muslim population there or not, nothing was done in contravention of the laws prescribed by the then-government of BH, especially because the republican staff of the TO established its own bylaws and then the TOs in the municipalities sent this down further to the local communes. So all of this was tied up in a system on the basis of this law, from top to bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 27 Mr. Sokolovic was mentioned. After your resignations he was the president of the Crisis Staff. Can you tell us from which party Mr. Sokolovic came?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: I think that that was an opposition party, something like the Democratic People's Party or something like that. At any rate, it was an opposition party close to the league of communists. He had his own members of the assembly and the SDP had their own. So he was not in the SDS party, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ujic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: If the Court allows me, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We do not usually hear the witnesses. Did you miss something, Mr. Ujic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, with the permission of the Court I would like to make a point of order or suggestion in relation to these two documents I have here, 0529758, and then further on up to 7589. These last two pages in this document should bear a different number according to the other document that I've received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- 05 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I don't follow what document he's referring to, Ms. Gustafson or Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't really know either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ujic, I don't think it's necessary for the Court. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how the witness got this document. He seemed to be citing an ERN number. I've looked it up. It is minutes from the 8th Session of the Rogatica Municipal Assembly. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As I told you, Mr. Ujic, that won't be necessary. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Will the Court allow me now in terms of my testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you may be excused. Thank you. Have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, shall we rise for ten minutes to give some time to Mr. Karadzic to absorb the Court ruling to redact some paragraphs from the statement in terms of his summary and the associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we're ready with the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- [Overlapping speakers]... adjusted, but the summary we could use -- need some time, but maybe we could bring the witness in and take as far as we can go and then reserve the lunch hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let us bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Banduka. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Tribunal. Under this rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the accused, the Prosecution, or the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you - and I'd like to remind myself - that we pause between our sentences so that sentences could be recorded in their entirety. And also could we pause between question and answer and then the next question. Did you provide a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up 1D08901 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the statement that you gave to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read it and did you sign it then?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that you're too close to the microphones because I thought that I was causing the microphone problem. Can we take a look at the last page and see whether that is your signature there.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the statement correctly reflect what you said? Would you correct anything in the statement?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I think it correctly reflects what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you suggest to the Defence team that in some paragraphs, for example, 33, 39, 47, there was a bit of imprecision?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes, I think some dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we take a look at paragraph 33 and then we would kindly ask you to tell us what should be changed there. Mr. Banduka, do you have a hard copy of your statement before you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. In paragraph 33 the date of the 12th of May does not correspond to what I said because the Muslim forces took this barracks on the 12th -- not on the 12th of May, but on the 10th of May. That's what we know. And also in a book that I read that was written by an officer of the BH Army, he also says that the barracks was taken on the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it should say the 10th of May rather than the 12th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the speaker, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Actually, I beg your pardon. I have it in my bag. Can I use it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear you, Mr. Karadzic, because your microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Sorry. I asked whether Mr. Banduka has his own statement, hard copy. So he said he did and asked for the permission to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem. By all means, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you found it, sir? Could you please take a look at paragraph 39 now. Is there something imprecise there?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. Again, the date. There is a reference to the documents that was issued by the Assembly of the Serb People and distributed -- it says that it was distributed after the 13th of March, and that is illogical because the Assembly was held on the 18th of April. So here instead of the 13th of March it should say after the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the word "after" is superfluous as well?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the sentence would read as follows: "The Assembly issued this document on the 18th of April, 1992, and distributed it ..." et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take a look at paragraph 47 now and tell us whether there is anything to be corrected in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I think that in line 3 all this confirmed our assessment at the time when they started leaving Hadzici en masse, that a strong attack was in the making and -- well, so we prepared. I think that that is superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did not say that; right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there anything else that you'd like to change in your statement or spell out in more specific terms?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I think that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Taking into account all of these things that you spelled out in more specific terms now, if I were to put the same questions to you today would your answers be the same in essence?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We really do have to pause. I have to tell you that a few paragraphs were redacted from the statement by the Trial Chamber because they're not relevant for the Defence, 59, 60, 62, and 63. So -- oh, there's more, 72 , 73, 75, 77, 78, so 78 included. That should not confuse you. These documents will not be part of this package either. Now I would like to read out the summary in the English language --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing so, we'll admit the Rule 92 ter statement first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2915, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it you are tendering five documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which were not on your 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. We would ask that they be added because at the time we hadn't interviewed this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did raise one issue with Mr. Robinson in advance which was the -- I believe that in paragraph 61 the -- there is a reference to P2297 which doesn't seem to support --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: -- the proposition. So perhaps if the document could be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because it was noted as already admitted, we didn't pay attention. But it seems to be referring to the document which was referred to in para 62 which is to be redacted. So we can leave it. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I think Registrar has been following the numbers. We'll admit those five associated exhibits. Shall we give the number in terms of following their order?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 01504 will be Exhibit D2916. 65 ter number 1D6706 will be Exhibit D2917. 65 ter number 1D3024 will be Exhibit D2918. 1D13027 will be Exhibit D2919. And 1D13028 will be Exhibit D2920.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, what about the summary and additional questions? Should we perhaps leave that for after the break in order to be clearer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if it is convenient. We'll take a break now for 45 minutes and resume at 14 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.27 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you hear me well, Mr. Banduka, in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll read out a summary of Mr. Banduka's statement in the English language. [In English] Vidomir Banduka was born on 9th of January, 1953, in Drozgometva, Hadzici municipality. He completed his elementary education in Hadzici, while he completed secondary school and the faculty of law in Sarajevo. During 1985, he went to work in a construction company, Ingrap of Hadzici, where he remained until the war broke out in 1992. Vidomir Banduka was a member of the VRS unit until 30 of December, 1992, at which time he was elected president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Hadzici municipality. He executed these duties until March 1996 when all inhabitants of Hadzici moved to Bratunac. After the Dayton Agreement, Hadzici remained in Federation. Before the war, Vidomir Banduka considered that the Muslims in Hadzici held -- considered that the Muslims in Hadzici held than the Serbs as they held many more important offices in the government and many were owners of the large companies were Muslims as they had the best connections with the central authorities. Due to this, a number of Serbs felt threatened and neglected. Vidomir Banduka was aware that the first political party to be formed was the SDA and the Serbs were the last to form their own political party. At the founding of the SDA, Mr. Banduka would estimate that there were approximately 4.000 people in attendance, whereas at the founding of the SDS there were about 100 people present. In the formation of the Municipal Assembly, Serbs were given less-influential positions than Muslims who were given key positions of responsibility. Following the formation of the Assembly, the SDA wanted to change everything that had been left over from the former system, including replacing personnel which the Serbs were opposed to. A large problem was the replacement of managerial staff in positions where they had no authorities, including schools and the health centres which were out of the competences of municipality authorities. In October 1991 the Serbian Assemblymen were forced to leave the Assembly due to significant misunderstandings and the Muslim politicians refusing to listen to the demands of the Serbian politicians and refused to work with them. The Serb politicians tried to inform the public about the problems they were faced with. They also tried to inform the public that all the decisions adopted by the Assembly in the coming period were not legal as they were being adopted without the participation of the Serbs. Only a small percentage of this was published as much of the media had sided with the SDA. The Assembly continued working for a short period after the Serbian Assemblymen left. The Muslims then established their own Defence Council instead. The Serbian municipality was established for a number of reasons. One factor was the disregard that the Muslim Assemblymen showed the Serbian. Further, the unrealistic mobilisation of Muslims in the reserve police force meant that many Serbian policemen left the police. Finally, due to the killing of a Serbian wedding guest in Bascarsija, many Serbs wished to establish a form of self-defence and the municipality was created to assist with this. People who were not members of the SDS were elected as president and deputy of the Serbian municipality. Vidomir Banduka considers that the war in Croatia had a negative effect on relations between people of different ethnicities and many Serbs noticed the number of the Muslim reserve policemen growing by the day with no explanations being provided by the Assembly. In addition, Muslims refused to be mobilised to JNA units and it became clear to Mr. Banduka and other Serbs that the Muslims and Croats were preparing for war. Vidomir Banduka received information that the Muslims had formed the Patriotic League and Green Berets as well as building their armed forces through the reserve police forces. He was aware that the police training school in Hadzici was training Muslim paramilitary units and Serbs were not allowed to enter the building. Further, the Muslim forces seized a number of army barracks and weapons depots arming the Muslim forces and in capturing the army barracks the Muslim soldiers killed members of the JNA. The only barracks under the control of the Serbian soldiers contained communication equipment and not armament. The MUP were also involved in the arming of the Muslims, providing them with further weaponry. War broke out on 24th of April in Ilidza, and following this the people in Hadzici decided to form a Crisis Staff to monitor and overcome the situation. On 8th of May, 1992, Muslims erected blockades at the entrance to the repairs depot in Hadzici and although they withdrew peacefully that night they fired upon surrounding settlements. By May Muslim civilians had left their homes in the centre of Hadzici and on 11th of May, the Muslims carried out a strong attack on the town centre. This indicated to Vidomir Banduka and the other Serbs that their departure had been previously planned. From this point on, Hadzici was under artillery fire every day from Muslim positions. The front lines of the fighting remained practically unchanged. In mid-May the JNA pulled out of BH and preparations for the formation of the VRS began which was formed on June -- in June 1992. Vidomir Banduka was only aware of one objective of the Bosnian Serbs: To defend their homes and families. On 16th of June, the Muslim forces attacked the village of Drozgometva, torching all of the houses. Elderly civilians remained in a neighbouring village and were killed and their homes torched. The Orthodox church in Pazaric was also set on fire. In light of these events, the Crisis Staff made the decision to create a holding centre, which would accommodate any remaining Muslim inhabitants. This centre was guarded to make the Muslim residents feel safer. The civilians in the centre were free to come and go as they pleased, but many returned because they felt safer. Detention of prisoners was governed by the Law on Criminal Procedure and this was adhered to by the police. At the beginning of the war, the Muslims formed camps where Serbs were held captive. During the war, Muslim forces cut off the supply of drinking water to the town as they controlled all sources of water. During 1993 a meeting was held to discuss water and electricity supplies and it was agreed that everyone should receive their services; however, the agreement was only in place for three days before the Muslims turned the water off again. Vidomir Banduka also found that of the most part of the war the telephone lines were not operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. Banduka. How much of the territory of Hadzici municipality was made part of the Serbian municipality of Hadzici? And what was the majority population in that part?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: In terms of percentages, I think it was about 20 per cent. It is the urban part of Hadzici plus a small number of neighbouring villages where the Serbs made up the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any intention or did you have any attempts carried out to place under control the Muslim part of Hadzici municipality?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think we ever made a step in that direction, be it by the army or anyone else, to change the situation as it had existed in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for the time being, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Banduka, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in most part in writing and you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd just like to start with a brief clarification. At paragraph 68 of your statement, you say that from July to December 1992 you were in the 4th Battalion as the assistant commander for moral guidance. I'd just like to clarify that that was the 4th Battalion of the Igman Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No. In the period of 1992 there were no four battalions when I was there. I think the brigade comprised two battalions. All of those who were mobilised from Hadzici were placed in one battalion. At first it was an independent battalion, and later, sometime in 1993, there was a restructuring process by which four battalions were created. In any case, it changes nothing important. In other words, I was serving with the battalion that defended Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Which, just to clarify, was part of the Igman Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. And the commander of the brigade while you were serving in it was Velimir Djindjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I've never heard of that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: What was the name of your commander?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: The commander was Mr. Velimir Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Banduka. I'm afraid it's a function of my poor pronunciation. I'll move on. In paragraph 28 of your statement you mentioned the Defence Council which convened instead of the Municipal Assembly after the Assembly stopped functioning. And you explained that this council mainly comprised Muslims and a few Serbs who they won over but who had not been elected by the Serbian people and did not represent the Serbs. Now, you attended this Defence Council only once, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: There is evidence before the Trial Chamber in this case from the TO representative on that Defence Council, Ramiz Dupovac, and for the reference of the parties that's P41, page 7 of the English and page B/C/S of the -- or page 8 of the B/C/S. Now, Mr. Banduka, Mr. Dupovac stated that on the council there was a representative from the army, the police, the TO, an representative from the administration services, the secretary of the secretariat for the people's defence, and further representatives from the delegates' clubs. So, in fact, this Defence Council was more representative than your statement would suggest, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, you are incorrect. I need to explain something first. The Defence Council was not elected or created by any official organ. They were self-proclaimed. The council was established by representatives of the Muslim side in the parliament once the Serbs had walked out in October 1991. Later on certain SDP members left although their party was multi-ethnic. In order to provide some kind of legitimacy because the Assembly no longer sat, they constituted that defence. That's what they called it. It doesn't exist in any documents. And this is the first time I hear from this statement that the people you mentioned attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Dupovac who actually attended the council, his evidence was that the SDS didn't refuse to participate in the functions of the council until mid-April. And, in fact, they used the Defence Council as a platform to emphasize their desire for Muslims and Serbs to have separate states. Mr. Banduka, did you -- were you aware of the SDS making public statements about their desire for Muslims and Serbs to have separate states?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, no. Ramiz Dupovac's statement, he was the deputy Chief of Staff of the TO on the Muslim side. He could say whatever he wanted, but that's not how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well again, something else that Mr. Dupovac said was that at one of the Defence Council meetings which he attended Ratko Radic, the president of the SDS Hadzici, stated in January 1992 that the Serbs didn't want to be in Alija's state and that separation and division was necessary and unavoidable. Were you aware of Mr. Radic publicly expressing this view?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No. That's Ramiz Dupovac's statement. He can say what he pleases.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'll move on. In paragraph 51 and 52 of your statement, you describe how at the very beginning of the war ordinary people got organised to defend their homes, villages [Realtime transcript read in error "religions"], and settlements, and you explain that preparations for the forming of the VRS began after the JNA had pulled out in mid-May 1992. And you contrast this situation with that of the Muslims which -- who you say had already formed their units. Now, earlier today you removed a reference in your statement to the Serbs making preparations in war -- or preparations for war in response to the Muslim departure from Hadzici and the Muslim attack on Hadzici. So I'd just like to clarify here what your evidence is. Is it your evidence that the Serbs in Hadzici began to arm themselves and prepare for war only after the JNA pulled out in mid-May 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No. You put a very long question which is also rather imprecise. How can I say that? The JNA withdrew from Bosnia on the 19th of May, if I recollect. Well, as early as the 11th of May there was a fierce attack on us, and by that day we already had at least a dozen dead. I'm afraid I did not fully comprehend your question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The Prosecution counsel is kindly requested to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I kindly ask that the Prosecutor indicate where it was stated that they were defending their faith?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think this must be an error in the transcript. If Mr. Karadzic could direct me to the relevant line of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's page 74 -- no, no, further up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I see the -- I see the mistake. The transcript says that Muslims -- or excuse me, the Serbs -- ordinary people got organised to defend their homes, religions, and settlements. In fact, I said homes, villages, and settlements. Thank you for that transcript correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, let's focus on this issue of the Serb organisation and arming in a bit more detail. First of all -- well, in your statement you describe in some detail how the Muslims in Hadzici armed themselves. And in paragraph 69 you state that the Serbs got most of their weapons from the TO, giving weapons -- or weapons were given to whoever responded to mobilisation. But focusing on the distribution of arms prior to the war, the Serbs also got weapons through the JNA, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, I'm unaware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, I'd like to direct your attention to your previous testimony on this topic in the Krajisnik case. If we could have 65 ter number 24574, please. And I would like to see page 123 of that document. And at lines 9 to 13 -- line 9 you were asked: "Q. Where did the Serbs get their weapons before the war? Where did the Serb people in your municipality get their weapons?" And you respond: "A. First through the reserve police. Whoever went to the reserve police got weapons. Whoever was a reservist of the JNA got weapons. Whoever was a member of the Territorial Defence got weapons." Mr. Banduka, do you accept that testimony as accurate?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes, but it runs contrary to the way you put your question. Your question was about the weapons provided by the JNA. This did not mean giving weapons to civilians. It was from the reserves of the JNA. Before the war, people were called up for the reserves. I was a reservist attending exercises, and whenever we did so I was issued with weapons. What I said is correct, but it only applied to those who were part of the reserve force of the then-official army, the JNA. That was the meaning of my words.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's look on that topic at a document that's in evidence before the Trial Chamber, that's P979. If we could have the first page of that document. Now, you'll see that this is a report authored by Milutin Kukanjac who was the commander of the JNA 2nd Military District, and it's dated 20th of March, 1992, and it is -- relates to the assessment of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And could we please move to page 6 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S. And what I'm interested in is heading number (5) which is entitled: "Volunteer forces in the 2nd Military District zone." And subsection (c) of that -- of that -- under that heading states: "No volunteers are potential conscripts for the regular units of the 2nd Army, and only a small number are from the TO of Bosnia and Herzegovina; in other words, the volunteer units are not part of the JNA and the TO establishment structure." And now, Mr. Banduka, if you direct your attention to subsection (f), that states that the JNA has distributed 51.900 weapons and the SDS 17.298. Finally, I'd like to move forward to page 11 in the English of this document and page 16 of the B/C/S. And here, Mr. Banduka, you'll see a table which explains the distribution of that total 69.198 arms that have been distributed by the JNA and the SDS by that date. And if you direct your attention to entry number 9 in that list, you'll see it states that 1500 men have been armed in the Hadzici municipality. So contrary to what you've just told us, this report shows that by the 20th of March, 1992, 1500 men who were not part of the JNA or the TO had been armed by either the JNA or the SDS in the Hadzici municipality. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the reference? Where does it say exactly that these men were under no obligation towards the JNA? First there is mention of volunteers and then elsewhere we are talking about the arming of JNA reservists. How can these two be correlated? Can we have the reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've just gone through -- Your Honours, we've just gone through the references which show that this is what this document evidences. I think it's a totally inappropriate intervention from Mr. Karadzic at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is it your question that this 1500 is number of the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 1500 is the number of people who were armed by either the JNA or the SDS in the Hadzici municipality who were not part of either the JNA or the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you may put the question. Mr. -- yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where do we see that in the text? That was what I think Dr. Karadzic is asking. That we have a table, but where in the text does it say what that table represents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She may put the question in such a way. And then having heard all the explanations, I think Mr. Banduka is able to answer the question. Let us see. Yes, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not able to see this figure either in the table or in your question, and I'm talking about the number of 1500. I don't know who was armed. Let me tell you this. The repair and maintenance depot had about 1.000 workers. All of them were treated as reservists of the JNA. There were also reservists in JNA barracks. All of those reservists were armed. Are you talking about those people? But on the other hand you say that the SDS was arming people. I was a member of the SDS and I know nothing about it, so I don't understand your assertion and your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, we'll come briefly to the issue of the SDS. We'll return to the issue of the SDS arming people. But just in order so that everybody understands, when you speak of -- in your statement you discussed the JNA's Zunovnica [sic] barracks and that Zunovnica was a village one or two kilometres outside of Hadzici town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: The name is Zunovica . You are confusing me with this mispronunciation and distracting me. Yes, there was the barracks there which was about 2 kilometres from the centre and in that barracks were some military assets stored and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And in that barracks there was -- it was a very large ammunition store spread over a very large complex; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And then in Hadzici town itself there was the maintenance and repairs depot, to which I think you just referred, which was also known as the TRZ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: The abbreviation is TRZ, which stands for "teknicko remintni zadno," repair and maintenance depot, and that was a company dealing with the maintenance/repair of weapons, but not only of weapons, of other equipment as well. They repaired heavy-duty vehicles, passenger cars, and other equipment, including armament.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. And so this TRZ made Hadzici town strategically important?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And so throughout the period of the conflict the Serbs controlled the TRZ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So again, just to focus on pre-war arming, and you speak about the -- at paragraph 32 of your statement you talk about the information that you had that in early 1992 the Muslims were removing weapons from the Zunovica army barracks. But it was the case, wasn't it, Mr. Banduka, that from mid-1991 the JNA in conjunction with the SDS were removing weapons from the Zunovica army barracks to arm the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: In my statement I wanted to describe the barracks. It was a huge area at the foot of Mount Igman. This is a rather forbidding terrain. And as far as I know, this barracks before the war was secured by very few soldiers. And unfortunately, it was accessible to anyone. So in that sense I said that from the back of the barracks that was leaning against Mount Igman, there were Muslim villages and they had easy access to the barracks, to put it in plain language there were thefts occurring in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: And then when the war broke out we took control of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's -- again, focusing on the period before the war, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence from Tihomir Glavas who was, as I'm sure you're aware, the commander of the public security station in Hadzici. And it was his testimony that the pre-war organisation of the Serb people by the SDS, including the distribution of weapons, functioned like clockwork.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And that's, for the parties' reference, is T11953 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So again, does this -- does this change your position on whether the SDS were involved in arming the Serbs prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. Tihomir Glavas' statement is a statement given by a policeman and I'm not in a position to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's focus on Ratko Radic who was the president of the SDS Hadzici; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, he was identified by Mr. Glavas as one of the main organisers of the weapons distribution to the Serbs. Were you aware of the role that he played in the pre-war arming of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, I know that the late Ratko Radic was the SDS president, but the opinion expressed by Tihomir Glavas about him is, again, something that I'm not willing to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's look at 65 ter 11283. And, Mr. Banduka, this is an SRK command report to the VRS Main Staff dated the 15th of December, 1993. If we can turn to page 3 of this document in both the English and the B/C/S. And you'll see in the first paragraph in the B/C/S and the fourth paragraph in the English version that Commander Galic is complaining about Mr. Radic, and he says: "Mr. President of municipality Hadzici was all the time interfering in managing and commanding at all levels of the VRS ..." And if you skip down halfway through that paragraph he states: "He can do it because he feeds and wears the army, he gives the apartments, and he partly organised the overtaking of the means from the stock of the former JNA, and the great number of warehouses were placed in the territory of municipality Hadzici, what he considers as his own means, not the State's and Republika Srpska Army's means." So here Mr. Radic's role in the pre-war arming of the Serbs in Hadzici is being acknowledged by Commander Galic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I don't know how you came to that conclusion. From this letter I see that Radic was making some requests and this Mr. Galic is asking the command or the Main Staff to do something. The late Mr. Radic was a rather stubborn person. He was an educated man, but he was rather harsh in some of his thinking and requests. I find it slightly odd that we have here a letter of a corps commander complaining about the conduct of a president. I find it strange.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, I'm going to have to ask you to listen carefully to my questions and answer them as precisely and concisely as possible. We're very limited in time and we have a lot to get through. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6109, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, can I please be told where it reads that this relates to the arming process before the war. I am looking for it but I cannot find it anywhere. I'm talking about Radic's involvement in the arming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think she mentioned arming with respect to this document. Did you, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document refers to Mr. Radic organising the overtaking of the means of the stock from the former JNA and the warehouses being placed in his territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where is that phrase?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It is halfway down in the large paragraph on page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was not before the war. It does not relate to the period before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, I'm going to move to a totally different subject. The armed conflict in Hadzici broke out on the 11th of May, 1992, and -- as you say in your statement. And in paragraph 46 you state that: "Until the 11th of May, 1992, the Muslims had left the centre of Hadzici. On the break of dawn of 11th of May, 1992, they launched a fierce attack on Hadzici. All this indicates that the departure of the Muslim inhabitants previously had been planned." In Krajisnik you testified that the Muslims left in the last few days before the 11th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And so the conflict which began in Sarajevo began at the beginning of May, around the -- on the 6th -- or, excuse me, the 6th of April, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I was in the centre of Sarajevo on 6th of April, 1992, but I wouldn't call it a conflict. I was free until the 25th of April to a TV building in Sarajevo which is some 30 kilometres from the place where I lived. Yes, it is true that there were some 10 or 15 roadblocks on the route, but I don't know if you can call that a conflict, the things that happened on the 6th of April in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, by the 11th of May we can agree that conflict had spread throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And, for example, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that on 8th of April, 1992, Foca was attacked by Serbs, resulting in Muslims freeing the area. Were you aware of -- were you aware of these events in Foca?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, were you aware of the attack on the Muslim commune of Zvrake [phoen] in Vogosca municipality on the 2nd to the 4th of May, resulting in Muslims being killed or expelled?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware because that's at least 20 kilometres from my place.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Okay. So from the 6th to the 8th of May you were celebrating your family feast day in your home in a village outside Hadzici town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that on the 7th of May the SDS issued an official ultimatum demanding that Muslim members of the police, the TO, and other illegal authorities and bodies leave the municipality and giving the Muslims a dead-line of 1800 hours on the 8th of May to leave the municipality. Were you aware that this ultimatum had been given?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, I don't think that such an ultimatum had ever been published. I don't know what is your source of information. It's probably somebody's statement or testimony, but I'm not aware of the existence of any such ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But, Mr. Banduka, you've just said that you -- during the relevant period you were outside of Hadzici town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So it's unsurprising in the circumstances of the pattern of killings and expulsions in neighbouring municipalities -- I put it to you that it's unsurprising that the Muslims took that ultimatum very seriously and departed Hadzici in response to it, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No. On the 22nd of April the Muslims attacked Ilidza to Kadic [phoen] off from Hadzici. So I can't see how it was possible for us to issue ultimatum to someone whilst the neighbouring municipality was already under attack which resulted in a large number of Serbs who were killed. So we were at the very end of Hadzici. Ilidza was attacked on the 22nd and you are now saying that we, just a handful of Serbs, issued an ultimatum to somebody. It is completely illogical.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, given the time constraints I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, I'm going to move on to the topic of the Hadzici sports centre. At paragraph 54 of your statement you say that: "The Crisis Staff set up a holding centre in the sports hall, seeing that the remaining Muslim inhabitants were complaining every day that they were experiencing difficulties due to the incensed atmosphere in the municipality and so the centre was set up to accommodate the people." And you say: "We did this because we thought it might be safer for them there since they would be guarded by the police and the army." Now, to begin with, you personally never visited the Hadzici sports centre when it was being used to accommodate Muslims, did you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, I never visited it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 56 you state that: "People came to the centre nearly every day of their own choosing because they felt safer there than in their own homes. Of course there were those who were persuaded to come because there were not enough policemen to guard every Muslim house." Now, you discussed these detention -- the detention centre, the sports centre, at some length in your Krajisnik testimony, but you never mentioned the fact that willing volunteers came nearly every day of their own choosing, did you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, I will have to say three sentences only before I answer your question. I already said in my statement the concept of the Muslim leadership prior to the outbreak of conflict to take out all the civilian population and then to attack us. And this was corroborated by the facts as well as by Dupovac's statement, that over the weekend during the course of a few days they all left the town and it was immediately followed by an attack. However, not all the residents left. They didn't obey the SDA or the Muslim leadership's instruction to leave the area. So some remained, and when the real conflict broke out, of course people felt extremely insecure because they realised that the war was really there. And just like I, they didn't believe that that would happen. So the majority of the Muslims who remained there and the war was already in progress, they also expressed a desire to cross over to the Muslim-held territory. So this collection centre is probably, we can call it, a transient point for them before crossing over to the Muslim-held territory. That's one of the reasons. The second reason was that Serb civilians were arriving from all areas between Zenica and Hadzici and Hadzici were the first stop on this area becoming vacant. You can imagine if somebody came from some other area because he was expelled by someone or he had some other reasons for leaving, he is afraid and he is looking for a place to stay where he could be safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, could you concentrate on answering the question. The question was not: What was the reason for the people coming? The question was why you didn't -- was that you didn't mention this in the testimony in Krajisnik case. Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, I did mention that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, turning then to the reason -- or sorry, focusing on this issue of whether people willingly went to the centre, it's your evidence today that people -- Muslim people willingly turned up at the centre nearly every day to be held there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Banduka, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence from a number of witnesses who were unwillingly taken to the Hadzici sports centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And just for the parties' references, I will refer to Witness Balic which is P161.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: He was taken to the centre on the 16th of May, 1992, after a brief period of house arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Witness Music, that's P2404. And Witness Okic, that's P125.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, none of these witnesses testified that they chose or, indeed, were persuaded to come to the centres. In fact, they were simply taken to the centres. Would you agree that a lot of people were simply taken to the centres, a lot of Muslim civilians were simply taken to the centres?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Your statement is a very serious one, taken away. After all, that is a war and talking about voluntariness in war and peace is a completely different matter. I'm saying that they were not taken there. Everything was done with the agreement of the people involved. Now, it depends on how people viewed this, whether they were taken or whether they were persuaded to do that but in agreement. That is something that I really cannot answer now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I think -- well, let me put Tihomir Glavas' evidence to you, which is that people were, indeed, taken from their houses by the Territorial Defence and the police. Again, there was no suggestion of voluntariness. Let me move on to the reasons people were detained at the sports centre. Now, one of the reasons people were detained was in order for them to be exchanged with Serb civilians; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, that was one of the reasons too. That is how people expressed their will, to come to the sports centre in order to be exchanged for a Serb family, a Serb civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before going further. You were asked, Mr. Banduka, about the evidence of Mr. Glavas that people were taken from their houses by the Territorial Defence and the police. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I am not aware of that statement of his and I don't see why you're asking me all the time to comment upon that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not recorded that the witness said in line 7, he is a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Banduka, this policeman testified that civilians were detained -- were arrested and detained at the sports centre in order for Serbs to have people to exchange. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that and I disagree with that. First of all, I don't have that statement. You keep asking me about this statement. You have it in front of you and I don't have it here. And I also don't have the statement of Glavas, the police commander, and I don't see why I would be commenting on his statement. I do not agree with his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about your own statement then. Paragraph 56, you say: "The Muslims who were in the holding centre could come freely in and out, having only to report to the policemen who were on guard." In fact, Mr. Banduka, the personnel who provided security for the centre had to give approval in order for anyone to leave, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So this wasn't merely a reporting requirement, was it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, if that policeman thought that it wasn't safe, Hadzici was being shelled every day by then, would it be safe for the policeman to let that someone go in a situation that was not safe, and then the other day he would be accused if anything were to happen to this person? We had people who were injured in front of the health centre, and it is only natural that if people were allowing others, giving permits, if you will, to leave, then they would have to take all of this into account. That is why they would have to address these policemen or whoever it was that was on guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So you accept that Muslim civilians were held against their will in the centres in the Hadzici sports centre?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let me refresh your recollection --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said you don't agree and you said something else. The interpreters did not catch it. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Or maybe we're not understanding each other. I don't know. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let me just refresh your recollection as to your testimony in Krajisnik on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And again that's 65 ter 24574. And if we could have page 157.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Yes, I'll read out the section and then the interpreters will translate. So you were asked: "And were" --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is for parties' references at line 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: "Q. And were Muslim civilians held against their will in the sports centre?" And you responded: "A. Well, I think that we can say yes, but we've already explained that, that it was for the purposes of protection." So there is no --

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. This was misinterpreted then. That's not what I said then, and I said this and I said "more or less," and then the Court asked me to clarify what I meant. No, no, no, I do not agree with this. I don't have the right translation here. I don't see how you are putting this to me, how you are saying that I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let me read you out the entirety of the passage. You said: "A. ... I think that we can say yes, but we've already explained that, that it was for the purposes of protection. Quite simply, even then people didn't believe that something could happen to them, something unexpected. So perhaps it's from that point of view that their will was not complied with." Mr. Banduka, in your testimony you're saying clearly -- in your Krajisnik testimony you said clearly that Muslim civilians were held against their will in the sports centre. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I do not agree. This is a surprise to me. That means that it was not translated properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's talk then about the protection that you say was afforded to the detainees in the centre. At paragraph 55 you say that: "In mid-June a group of hooligans arrived at the sports centre and abused the detainees." And you say: "As far as I know there were no other cases other than this one." Now, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence from Witness Misic, that's P2403 , at paragraph 63, that paramilitaries came twice to the sports centre, once on the 25th of May and once on the second day of Bajram. And from Witness Balic, and that's at P161, and again he states that around 1st of June, 1992, three Arkanovci came to the sports centre and 15 days later some Seseljevci came and abused and beat the prisoners. In fact, Mr. Banduka, prisoners were abused in the Hadzici sports centre on multiple occasions, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Let me tell you, by the way, since you mentioned Witness Nisic and he says on the second day of Bajram: The second day of Bajram was the 8th of April. There was no war then. And Bajram was on the 6th of April, as far as I can remember, in Sarajevo, and they celebrated that, and how, in Sarajevo. And then there was this one incident when Balic was beaten up. I really am not aware of any other incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The Hadzici civilian authorities had a reputation for being permissive and allowing crimes to occur, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P1507.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, this is an SRK report from Commander Sipcic to the VRS Main Staff and it's dated the 13th of July, 1992. And if we could move to page -- or paragraph 3, if we could focus on paragraph 3, Commander Sipcic says: "The situation in the territory of the corps continues to be complex. Cases of looting, murder, and various misappropriations of funds have occurred. In trying to prevent such occurrences, the security organs and the military police are coming up against strong resistance and individual organs of civilian authority (Ilidza, Hadzici)." Do you agree that this document shows that the Hadzici civilian authorities had a reputation of allowing a crime -- for allowing crimes to occur?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, what is said here is looting and killings? Which killings? Maybe a Serb can kill a Serb. There were such cases too. My goodness. It's not that what is stated here is that it is the killing of Muslims that is being tolerated or of the other side. And also, this is just the personal position taken by a particular officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Banduka. I'd like to move on to the municipality building and at paragraph 57 of your statement you say that one floor on the -- one room on the ground floor was used for detention. Can you just confirm that the Crisis Staff and subsequently the Municipal Assembly was located on the second floor of that same building; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 58 you say that: "No one could stay in the police detention room in the municipality building for over a month because of the Law on Criminal Procedure. If there was a need to hold them for longer, they would be transferred to Kula."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to call up P1607, please. And just while this document is being called up, if I could have page 2 in the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This -- this is a report dated the 22nd of October, 1992, on the situation in prisons and collection camps for prisoners of war, and it's a report by Slobodan Aviljas who was a representative of the Republika Srpska Ministry of Justice and administration. Now, if we could focus on section 10 of this report which is at page 6 to 7 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S -- sorry, that would be the -- yeah, thank you. The first paragraph in this section states: "Ninety prisoners of war are accommodated in the Hadzici sports centre. Organisation and security is provided by the Hadzici public security station ..." And then the final paragraph in that section which is on page 6 of the B/C/S, I believe, states: "In the cases of Zvornik, Hadzici, and Ilidza, we see that public security stations keep people in custody without any authorisation or justification in law because they have the authority to keep people in custody for no longer than three days." Mr. Banduka, in fact, the limit on detention without justification under the law was three days, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I mean, that's the way it is according to the present-day law I think, but I think that then people could be kept for up to a month. Also, in addition to that, we did not have the right conditions. We'd have to cross the airport area to get to Kula, the proper institution for that. So there were many difficulties involved in terms of transferring persons from Hadzici to Kula. I would also be interested in the date. This document is from which date?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This document is from the 22nd of October, 1992, and let's move forward to a letter of that same date from the -- and this is -- sorry, this is English page 88 and B/C/S page -- excuse me, English page 28 and B/C/S page 27.
